Deep ALMA imaging is thus essential to detect PMC disks and examine their physical properties.
Here we report the discovery of 0.88 mm continuum emission at the position of SR 12 c.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS$/$JAO.ALMA $\#$2019.1.01212.S.

We report an Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array 0.88 mm (Band 7) continuum detection of the accretion disk around SR 12 c, an $\sim$11 $M_{\rm Jup}$ planetary-mass companion (PMC) orbiting its host binary at 980 au.

The ALMA Band 7 observations of SR 12 were carried out on UT 2021 July 8–11, with three 2 GHz windows centered at 333.791, 335.741, and 347.741 GHz, and one 0.938 GHz window centered at 345.787 GHz to image ${}^{12}$CO (3–2) at a resolution of 0.488 MHz.

The ALMA Band 7 observations of SR 12 were carried out on UT 2021 July 8–11, with three 2 GHz windows centered at 333.791, 335.741, and 347.741 GHz, and one 0.938 GHz window centered at 345.787 GHz to image ${}^{12}$CO (3–2) at a resolution of 0.488 MHz.
The size and the position angle of the synthesized beam are $0.147\ensuremath{''}\times0.090\ensuremath{''}$ and 104.0$^\circ$.
The disk is not resolved with Briggs weighting (robust $=$ 0.5) in `tclean` either, where the beam size is $0.108\ensuremath{''}\times0.066\ensuremath{''}$.
The rms in the CO-free channels of 1 km s$^{-1}$ width is $\sim$0.7 mJy beam$^{-1}$.
We adopted natural weighting for a better S$/$N and used the CASA task `tclean` to generate the final continuum map (Figure 1), which has an rms of 10 $\mu$Jy beam$^{-1}$ around the map center.
Dust continuum from the host binary is not detected down to an rms of 19 $\mu$Jy beam$^{-1}$, which is consistent with results from (cite: MK21) that the binary has no Spitzer infrared excess.
The total on-source time is 10,705 s (2.97 hr).

This is slightly different from the positions of SR 12 c in Gaia DR2 ($16^{\mathrm{h}}27^{\mathrm{m}}19.659s$, $-24\ensuremath{^\circ}41\ensuremath{'}49.22\ensuremath{''}$; epoch J2015.5) and EDR3 ($16^{\mathrm{h}}27^{\mathrm{m}}19.658s$, $-24\ensuremath{^\circ}41\ensuremath{'}49.24\ensuremath{''}$; epoch J2016), but as demonstrated in Figure 2, after accounting for the Gaia DR2 proper motion of the host binary ($\mu_{\alpha^\ast} = -7.7\pm1.1$ mas yr$^{-1}$, $\mu_\delta = -25.3\pm0.8$ mas yr$^{-1}$), the expected position of SR 12 c at the time of our observations matches the position of this 0.88 mm source.

The SED fitting in (cite: SM18) yields a spectral type of L$0\pm1$, log *g* $=4\pm0.5$, and an effective temperature of $2600\pm100$ K, so the radius of SR 12 c using the Stefan–Boltzmann law is expected to be about 1.6 $R_{\rm Jup}$.

X-shooter spectroscopy in (cite: SM18; SM19) reveals multiple hydrogen lines, in particular the prominent H$\alpha$ emission, indicating that SR 12 c is accreting at a rate of $10^{-11.08\pm0.40}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$.

Using the Gaia DR2 distance, the *J*-band bolometric correction in (cite: Filippazzo15), and the models in (cite: Baraffe15), we find a slightly lower bolometric luminosity of log$(L/L_{\odot})=-2.95\pm0.11$ dex and a mass of $11\pm3~M_{\rm Jup}$.

It is about 1.5 times brighter than the CPD around PDS 70 c (86 $\mu$Jy; (cite: B21)) given their very similar distances (112.5 pc to SR 12 and 112.4 pc to PDS 70).
We find a mean disk temperature of 29 K for the PDS 70 c disk when integrating $T(r)$ to 1 au, the disk outer radius constrained by (cite: B21).

Another planetary-mass object whose disk has been detected by ALMA is OTS 44 (2MASS J11100934$-$7632178), a free-floating $\sim$12 $M_{\rm Jup}$ object accreting at $7.6\times10^{-12}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ (cite: J13).
Its disk has a 1.3 mm flux density of 101 $\mu$Jy (cite: B17), translating to 238 $\mu$Jy at 0.88 mm assuming a spectral index of 2.2 (cite: Ribas17).

Adopting a Gaia DR2 distance of 192 pc to the Chamaeleon I star-forming region (cite: Dzib18) and assuming the same $T_{\rm mean}$ and opacity as the SR 12 c disk,[^6] we find a dust mass of 0.064 $M_\oplus$ (5.2 $M_{\rm Moon}$) with $\kappa_{\rm 1\, mm}$ and 0.295 $M_\oplus$ (24 $M_{\rm Moon}$) with $\kappa_{\rm 1\, \mu m}$.
Such an assumption may be expected for PMC disks as the simulations in (cite: Rab19) show that PMC disks are optically thick at millimeter wavelengths.
